events.name: Tet (Vietnamese Lunar New Year)
events.recurrence_note: Annual lunar holiday; official public holiday length and exact dates vary by year.
events.date_note: 2026 dates are an operational planning window and should be verified against official holiday notices before travel.
events.traveler_summary: Tet is Vietnam's most important holiday and can affect transport, restaurants, shops, banking, tours, and hotel availability.
events.cultural_context: Families gather, homes are cleaned and decorated, ancestors are honored, and many people travel before and after the holiday.
practical_guidance: Book trains, domestic flights, sleeper buses, and hotels well ahead of the holiday period.
Carry extra cash before closures, because banks and some small businesses may close.
Check restaurant and tour availability directly for the days before, during, and after Tet.
etiquette_notes: Avoid negative comments about family traditions or holiday spending.
Be patient with slower service and reduced hours.
Respect private family gatherings and home rituals.

events.name: Reunification Day
events.date_note: Often connects with International Labour Day on May 1 for a longer domestic travel period.
events.traveler_summary: Reunification Day can create national holiday crowds, public events, and heavier domestic travel, especially around major cities and beaches.
events.cultural_context: The day marks the end of the war in 1975 and is connected to national memory and reunification narratives.
practical_guidance: Expect heavier travel demand around April 30 and May 1.
Keep comments around war history factual and respectful.
Avoid protests, political gatherings, or heated public debate.
etiquette_notes: Treat flags, ceremonies, and public commemorations respectfully.
Avoid joking about war history or national symbols.

events.name: National Day
events.date_note: Official holiday arrangements can create adjacent days off depending on the year.
events.traveler_summary: National Day can bring fireworks, ceremonies, domestic trips, crowding, and some public-service schedule changes.
events.cultural_context: The holiday commemorates Vietnam's declaration of independence and is a national pride moment.
practical_guidance: Expect crowds around central squares, fireworks viewpoints, and waterfront areas.
Plan extra time for taxis and ride-hailing near major events.
Treat national symbols and official ceremonies respectfully.
etiquette_notes: Do not climb on monuments, flags, or official decorations.
Avoid sarcastic or insulting public posts about the holiday or national symbols.

events.name: Mid-Autumn Festival
events.recurrence_note: Annual lunar festival, usually in September or October.
events.date_note: Confirm the lunar date each year.
events.traveler_summary: The Mid-Autumn Festival brings lantern displays, family activities, mooncakes, and evening crowds in many cities.
events.cultural_context: In Vietnam, the festival is closely associated with children, lanterns, family gatherings, and traditional performances.
practical_guidance: Expect evening crowds in old quarters, pedestrian streets, and riverside areas.
Book restaurants earlier around popular viewing districts.
Be careful photographing children and families; ask or avoid close-up images without consent.
etiquette_notes: Do not push through lantern processions or children's performances.
Keep photography respectful around families and religious offerings.

events.name: Hoi An Lantern Festival
events.recurrence_note: Usually associated with full-moon evenings in Hoi An Ancient Town.
events.date_note: Confirm monthly dates locally before planning around it.
events.traveler_summary: Hoi An's lantern evenings can create dense foot traffic around the old town and riverside.
events.cultural_context: Lantern traditions are tied to Hoi An's trading history and local heritage identity.
practical_guidance: Arrive early if you want riverside photos or restaurant seating.
Expect walking-only or controlled access in parts of the old town.
Keep belongings close in dense crowds.
etiquette_notes: Avoid blocking narrow lanes for long photo sessions.
Respect religious offerings and private homes in heritage streets.

sensitivity_notes.title: War History Awareness
sensitivity_notes.traveler_summary: War history is visible in museums, memorials, tours, and family memories; travelers should keep the tone respectful and factual.
sensitivity_notes.why_it_matters: The same events may be described differently depending on national, family, and international context.
avoid: Making jokes or staged content at war museums, tunnels, cemeteries, or memorials.
Arguing with guides, staff, or locals about terminology in public settings.
Filming grieving visitors, veterans, or ceremonies without consent.
practical_safe_behavior: Use neutral, factual language when discussing history in public.
Listen first when guides or locals explain their perspective.
Keep sensitive debates private and away from memorial spaces.
examples: At the War Remnants Museum, avoid performative photos and keep commentary measured.
On a Cu Chi tunnel tour, ask questions respectfully rather than challenging the guide in front of a group.

sensitivity_notes.title: Political Gatherings and Protest Sensitivity
sensitivity_notes.traveler_summary: Travelers should avoid demonstrations, political gatherings, and filming police or security activity.
sensitivity_notes.why_it_matters: Crowds connected to political issues can draw official attention and may move quickly from ordinary public activity to a sensitive situation.
avoid: Joining or lingering near protests or political gatherings.
Filming police, military, checkpoints, government buildings, or security incidents.
Posting real-time commentary that frames local authorities or public events in inflammatory terms.
practical_safe_behavior: Leave the area calmly if a crowd becomes political or tense.
Follow police or security instructions without arguing.
Check official travel advice before travel and during major events.
examples: If a march blocks a street, take a different route rather than recording from the front line.
If stopped near a government building, stay calm, show documents if requested, and avoid jokes or arguments.
sensitivity_notes.source_label: U.S. Department of State Travel Advisory

sensitivity_notes.title: Temples, Pagodas, and Religious Sites
sensitivity_notes.traveler_summary: Temples, pagodas, shrines, and family altars should be treated as active spiritual spaces.
sensitivity_notes.why_it_matters: Dress, photography, noise, and body language can affect worshippers and caretakers.
avoid: Pointing feet at altars, statues, monks, or offerings.
Touching offerings, statues, bells, or ritual objects without permission.
Taking close-up photos of worshippers or monks without consent.
practical_safe_behavior: Dress modestly and cover shoulders or knees where requested.
Remove shoes or hats where posted or when locals do so.
Keep voices low and step aside for worshippers.
examples: At a pagoda, stand to the side rather than directly in front of someone praying.
If shoes are lined outside a hall, remove yours before entering.

sensitivity_notes.title: Face-Saving, Bargaining, and Public Disagreement
sensitivity_notes.traveler_summary: Keeping interactions calm and polite is important in markets, taxis, hotels, restaurants, and public spaces.
sensitivity_notes.why_it_matters: Public anger, humiliation, or aggressive bargaining can escalate a small disagreement and make help less likely.
avoid: Shouting, pointing aggressively, or filming someone during a dispute.
Calling a person a scammer or liar in public without stepping back first.
Refusing to move aside when staff are trying to resolve a queue or payment issue.
practical_safe_behavior: Use a calm tone and simple language when negotiating.
Step aside from crowds before resolving payment or booking issues.
Use hotel staff, app support, or written receipts when communication breaks down.
examples: If a market price feels too high, smile, decline, and walk away rather than arguing.
If a ride price changes, compare the app or written quote calmly before deciding.

sensitivity_notes.title: National Symbols and Pride
sensitivity_notes.traveler_summary: Flags, monuments, leaders, independence history, and national celebrations should be treated respectfully.
sensitivity_notes.why_it_matters: Careless jokes or insulting content about national symbols can offend locals and attract unwanted attention.
avoid: Climbing on monuments, official decorations, or war memorials.
Using flags, uniforms, or official symbols as props for jokes.
Posting insulting or mocking comments about national holidays or symbols.
practical_safe_behavior: Observe ceremonies from an appropriate distance.
Keep social posts factual and respectful around national topics.
Follow posted rules at monuments, museums, and government areas.
examples: At a public square on National Day, do not climb barriers or decorations for photos.
At a museum, summarize exhibits neutrally rather than using mocking captions.
